Eleanor Hartwell stood at the lighthouse window, watching the storm gather over the bay.
The old keeper had warned her that the lamp room would be coldest just before the squall hit.
Below her, the village of Marston Cove had already extinguished its harborside lanterns.
The Linden, a fishing schooner returning late from the northern banks, had not yet cleared the rocks.
Eleanor traced the shoreline with her brass scope, counting the seconds between thunderclap and flash.
Her grandfather had built this lighthouse with his own hands during the winter of eighteen-seventy-two.
The original fresnel lens had been replaced once in nineteen-twenty-four, after a shipment of Welsh glass arrived.
Three keepers had served before her: Marcus Alden, his son Theodore, and finally her own father, Daniel Hartwell.
Each keeper had kept a logbook of weather, ships sighted, and small private notes on the loneliness of the work.
Eleanor had read every entry, beginning when she was nine years old and her father was teaching her the trade.
The Linden's captain, an old friend of her father, would have his crew clinging to the windward rail by now.
She lit the secondary signal, a green flare that meant 'beware the eastern shoals' to any ship within five miles.
The cottage at the foot of the lighthouse was warm, banked with peat, and her sister Margaret was inside.
Margaret had returned from Edinburgh in spring, after seven years studying maritime engineering at the university.
She brought books, sextants, and a small ledger of weather patterns she had compiled from harbor records.
The two sisters had agreed that Margaret would handle the daylight watch, Eleanor the night shift.
Their cousin Thomas, a marine biologist working out of Bergen, sent letters every fortnight describing his fieldwork.
Thomas studied seals; specifically the migration of grey seals along the Faroese rookeries each autumn.
The lighthouse was on a thin spit of granite that locals called the Tongue, surrounded by deep water on three sides.
Eleanor noted the wind direction in her own logbook: east-northeast at thirty knots, rising.
A flock of guillemots had taken shelter in the rock crannies below the lamp room, unusual for this season.
The barometer had fallen three points in the last hour, a steeper drop than any she had witnessed.
She thought of her father's last logbook entry, written four years ago on the night he had died at sea.
He had been aboard the Linden then, helping bring the boat home through a smaller storm than this one.
Eleanor had been sixteen, away at school, and learned of his death from a telegram delivered by the postmaster.
The lighthouse had been hers since then, by a clause in his will that surprised even the town magistrate.
A faint light appeared off the southern point — the Linden, finally clearing the headland into deeper water.
Eleanor watched the schooner heel hard to port, fighting the swell, every plank visible in the lamp's beam.
She held her breath as the boat passed the line of breakers, then slipped into the relative shelter of the bay.
The crew on deck waved their lanterns three times — the keeper's signal, an acknowledgement of the warning.
Eleanor returned the signal with the lamp itself, two long flashes and one short, the family code.
She closed the logbook, set down the scope, and descended the spiral iron staircase to the cottage below.
Margaret had brewed tea, and the kettle whistled faintly from the kitchen at the end of the hall.
Outside, the storm broke fully over the lighthouse, but the lamp turned steadily on, indifferent to the weather.
The night would be long, but the Linden was safe, and the lamp would not falter before dawn.
